primitives.name: Abstract System Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: Computer simulation or a computer model has the task to simulate an abstract model of a particular or equivalent system.
primitives.assumptions: The system is representable as a deterministic or stochastic process with identifiable inputs and outputs.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the abstraction fails to capture essential dynamics or when input space exceeds model capacity.

layer2.mapping: GSI Bayesian inference treats model outputs as likelihood functions; GSE state-transition graphs encode temporal evolution of system states.
layer2.telemetry: Model accuracy metrics, cross-validation error rates

primitives.name: Computational Experimentation
primitives.verbatim_quote: Firstly, the simulation of the real system should be made, and after that, if the simulation gives satisfactory results, realization of previously examined system can be carried out.
primitives.assumptions: Simulation results approximate real-world behavior within acceptable tolerance bounds.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When experimental design lacks sufficient variability or when model misalignment leads to spurious outcomes.

layer2.mapping: GSE uses derived kernels to map simulation trajectories into actionable decision policies; GSI applies kernel density estimation to infer latent variables.
layer2.telemetry: Statistical significance of simulation outcomes, convergence diagnostics

primitives.name: Input-Output Behavior
primitives.verbatim_quote: In order to have a useful model, it is necessary to determine its behavior for defined and limited set of variables.
primitives.assumptions: System response is governed by a finite set of controllable and observable parameters.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When external noise or unmodeled interactions dominate internal dynamics.

layer2.mapping: GSI infers conditional probability distributions from input-output pairs; GSE evaluates control policies based on expected utility across input domains.
layer2.telemetry: Mean squared error between predicted and actual outputs, entropy of response distribution

reasoning_traces.think:
The foundational principle of computer simulation lies in constructing an abstract representation of a real system that mirrors its essential behaviors under controlled conditions. This abstraction allows for repeated experimentation without physical constraints, enabling predictive modeling. From a mathematical standpoint, this process involves defining a mapping from input variables to output responses, often expressed as a function f(X) = Y where X represents environmental or operational inputs and Y denotes system outputs. The validity of such mappings depends on the fidelity of the underlying model assumptions—typically grounded in differential equations, statistical distributions, or graph-theoretic structures. In GSI, these mappings are interpreted through Bayesian inference frameworks, where prior beliefs about system parameters are updated via observed simulation data. Conversely, GSE employs similar structures but focuses on dynamic state transitions governed by temporal logic and probabilistic automata. The dual nature of simulation thus manifests in two distinct yet complementary lenses: one emphasizing epistemic uncertainty (GSI) and the other focusing on operational dynamics (GSE). Failure modes arise when the model's domain of applicability is exceeded, leading to extrapolation errors or catastrophic misalignment between theoretical constructs and empirical reality.
